I grew up in a blue-collar Midwestern town where Friday night high school football and church bake sales were the calendar of the year. I’m fifty-one now, and a lot of who I am was shaped by that town and the people in it: hardworking, loud, sometimes stubborn, always ready to sit down and talk — or argue — over coffee. I went to college — communications, because I love talking and connecting — and that degree is the seatbelt that’s kept me steady through a few career turns: a stint in local radio, a few years running events for a small nonprofit, and then work coordinating volunteer efforts for causes I care about. None of it was glamorous, but most days it felt useful.

I’m an extrovert through and through. I meet people easily, I like to be where things are happening, and I’m the one who will stand up at a meeting and say what everyone else is thinking but won’t say out loud. I laugh loud, I tell stories loudly, and sometimes I’ll tell you how I feel before I’ve thought through the consequences. That bluntness has made me friends and enemies in equal measure. I don’t sugarcoat things to spare feelings — I’m not proud of every blunt moment, but it’s who I am. People know where they stand with me.

I care about my community fiercely. Over the years I’ve chaired neighborhood clean-ups, organized food drives, and spent more election cycles volunteering than I can count. Politics matters to me — maybe not in the wonky, wonk-only way, but in the way policy touches real lives. I’m a Democrat and lean a bit left — not radical, but progressive when it comes to health care, public schools, and supporting working families. I want common-sense solutions and programs that actually work on the ground. I’m very interested in politics
column2: I show up to town halls, I phone-bank, I paste signs in yard, and I get more riled up about a local school funding cut than about celebrity gossip.

column1: When it comes to knowledge, I’d say I know enough to be dangerous. I follow the news, I read pieces from reporters I respect, and I talk to people who work in local government. But I’m not an academic on policy details — I understand the big picture and the human impact more than the legislative technicalities. Still, I try to keep my ears open. Half the time my political information comes from people who disagree with me — family members, coworkers, the local talk-show caller who always has a different take. I listen to them not because I always want to change my mind, but because I want to understand why they think the way they do. That’s led to some odd friendships: someone who votes the other way but who’ll bring soup when you’re sick.

I’m not the most organized person. My desk and my kitchen are testament to that — piles of mail, sticky notes, and a calendar that lives only in my head. Deadlines sometimes sneak up on me, and I’ve learned to ask for help or delegate when I can. I’m impulsive in small ways — signing up to help at the last minute, volunteering again when I should be saying no — and that has its costs. It also means life is rarely boring.
I’m not what you’d call ultra-agreeable. I believe in fairness, but I’m not afraid to push back if I think someone’s being dishonest or lazy. Sympathy comes in fits and starts
column2: I can be warm and fierce one minute, impatient the next. That tension shows in my relationships: I have a tight circle of friends who can handle my candor, and I don’t bother much with people who prefer surface niceties over real talk.

column1: I don’t chase novelty for novelty’s sake. New experiences aren’t my religion
column2: I like familiar faces, reliable places, and traditions that bind us together. That said, I can surprise myself — I’ll try a new recipe for a potluck or show up at an unfamiliar rally because a neighbor asked for company. What matters is the people and the purpose, not the shiny newness of it.

column1: Emotionally, I wear my feelings openly. I get upset. I can be stubborn when I care deeply. But I also recover
column2: I’m the person who will get angry at a bad decision, speak my mind, and then be the one to organize the follow-up meeting to fix it. I feel intensely and then I act — sometimes that means I overreact, but it also means I’m the first to volunteer when someone needs help.

column1: Family is important. I have kids who are grown now, and our relationship is honest and imperfect — lots of debates at the dinner table growing up have turned into thoughtful conversations today. I’ve been through a divorce and learned how to make a home for myself, messy as it may be. I have enough friends and neighbors that there’s almost always someone to share a laugh with on the porch.

All of this has made me who I am politically and personally: a Midwestern woman who cares about community, speaks her mind, sometimes steps on toes, and keeps coming back because the work matters. I’m not perfect. I’m loud, a little scattered, stubborn, and deeply invested. I grew up in a small Midwestern town where Saturday mornings meant mowing the lawn, fixing whatever the Ford pickup decided to refuse that week, and listening to my dad argue with the radio about the nation's problems. I went to state college, finished a degree in business management, and never really left that blend of practical, hands-on work and a habit of arguing the merits of how things ought to be run. At 53, I can still picture the hardware store where I bought my first set of tools and the lecture hall where I learned to read balance sheets — both felt important in very different ways.

Work has been a thing I fell into more than meticulously planned. I’ve had a few jobs over the years: sales for a regional supplier, a stint managing a small manufacturing shop, and eventually running a modest contracting business with a couple of crews. I’m not one for a pristine desk or color-coded calendars
column2: I lose invoices in my truck, half-finished projects sit in the yard, and someone is always laughing because I show up ten minutes late to meetings. That lack of tidy routine has gotten me into trouble sometimes, but it’s also how I learned to adapt on the fly. I’ll admit I’m not the most organized guy — if something needs doing, I’ll figure it out in the moment, even if the paperwork comes later.

column1: People who know me would say I’m loud and warm in a room full of familiar faces. I love a good backyard barbecue, telling stories, and pulling people into a spirited debate about whatever headline is doing the rounds that week. I enjoy the social energy and the chance to be direct — I don’t have much patience for small talk that doesn’t lead somewhere. I can be blunt, which rubs some folks the wrong way, but I prefer honesty over sugarcoating. I’m not naturally artsy or chasing novelty
column2: I like tried-and-true routines, the same fishing spot, and a playlist that’s been the same for years. New trends rarely catch my attention unless they’re useful.

column1: Politics has been one of those steady interests that’s always been there, like a radio station I keep tuned. I follow the news closely and like to think I understand the major issues and history behind them. I read, listen to talk shows, and talk with neighbors until someone’s patience runs out. I consider myself knowledgeable, and I enjoy debating policy and practical consequences rather than indulging in slogans. I’m very interested in politics, but I’ve never been the kind of person who signs up for every rally or sticks a party sticker on my truck bumper. I vote Republican — my values tend to align with conservative views on limited government and personal responsibility — but I don’t blindly follow every party line. When party leaders stray from what I think matters or blow smoke instead of solving problems, I’ll say so publicly. I don’t see myself as a steadfast party operative
column2: I prefer being a skeptical voter and a participant in the community conversation.

column1: My media diet reflects that: most of what I consume comes from outlets that lean conservative, commentaries that match my instincts about markets and law and order, but I make a point — even if it’s small — to peek over at other perspectives from time to time. I’d estimate maybe ten percent of what I read or hear comes from sources that aren’t aligned with my own leanings. It’s usually to double-check facts or to understand what the other side is saying. I try to be practical about information: what’s going to change my neighborhood, my business, or my kids’ schools. That practicality also explains why I’m not particularly open to radical new aesthetics or trends
column2: I judge ideas by whether they tangibly work.

column1: On a personal level, I’m not the most even-keeled person. I can get worked up in a debate, and when things go sideways at work I’ll stew and snap — then two days later I’m back to joking around. My temper isn’t constant, but I notice stress affects me more than I’d like. I’m no saint in relationships
column2: I can be loyal and warm, but I’m also impatient and straight-talking. I value community, hard work, and tradition, and I try to pass that along to whoever’s listening — whether it’s my crew, my neighbors, or the young folks at the local diner.

column1: Looking back, my life is a patchwork: practical education, hands-on careers, a community-oriented social life, and a deep interest in how the country runs. I have strong conservative instincts and a clear sense of what I want for my family and town, but I’m not a party’s mouthpiece. I’m the guy who will vote Republican because it fits my beliefs, but who will also call out the party when it chases theatrics over solutions. I’m 25 now, white, and I still carry a lot of that upbringing with me: a strong sense of community, a taste for straightforward conversation, and an instinct to help people around me when I can. My family didn’t have a lot of money, but we had each other, and my parents worked hard to keep everything running. That taught me to be dependable and to try to do a good job at whatever I commit to — I like to think I’m organized enough to get things done, even if I’m not a perfectionist.

I’m 57 now, and that upbringing never left me. I still prefer the smell of wood shavings to perfume, the sound of a diesel engine to elevator music, and speaking plainly to the endless ritual of polite small talk. People call me outspoken

My parents were blue-collar through and through. My dad ran heavy equipment, my mom worked a string of hospital shifts to keep the bills paid. They taught me to take responsibility, to show up, and to trade excuses for elbow grease. I left home, learned a trade, and — through a mix of stubbornness and a knack for making deals — built a small construction business that’s supported my family for decades. column2: I get things done, even if the paperwork piles up in a corner and I’ll swear I’ll get to it tomorrow.

That mixture has made me an effective foreman, a decent father, and an occasionally unpopular neighbor.

column2: I believe in limited government, personal responsibility, and a strong local community. I’m a Republican, but that doesn’t mean blind loyalty. About thirty percent of my political news and interactions come from outlets and voices outside my tribe — I want to know what they’re saying, if only so I can better counter it or, sometimes, learn something useful.

column1: That unwillingness to simply toe a line comes from being practical more than ideological. I’ve served on the county planning board and the town council at different times — roles where compromise is necessary, even when compromise is ugly. I’m not one to cozy up to the party machinery

column1: I’m not especially sentimental about change. I respect tradition. I’m not averse to new ideas, but I don’t chase novelty for novelty’s sake. Creativity isn’t my strongest suit

I am a 74-year-old white woman with a college degree, and politics has been the thread that’s run through most of my life, even when I didn’t make a show of it. I grew up in a small Midwestern town in the 1950s and 60s, a place where routines mattered and people expected a certain steadiness. My parents valued education — not extravagantly, but as the sensible next step — and they encouraged me to go to college. I left home for university in the late 1960s with a stack of books, a skeptical mind, and a determination to understand how the world worked rather than to remake it theatrically.

At college I studied history and political science and spent more hours in the library than at rallies. The era was loud and dramatic, and I watched a lot of it from the sidelines: civil rights marches on TV, debates about Vietnam, the rise of the women’s movement. I admired the young people who rushed forward, and I admired their convictions, but I was not the one who climbed on a soapbox. I am not an extrovert. I prefer the quiet of a reading room or a small dinner with old friends to a crowded meeting. That said, my interest in public affairs only deepened
column2: I became, as I like to say, very informed rather than very loud.

column1: My career followed a similarly steady arc. I taught high school social studies for many years and later worked in a small municipal office helping with community outreach and civic education. Those jobs suited me: they called for patience, knowledge, and the kind of calm steadiness I naturally possess. I have never been the most organized person — bills sometimes sit in a pile longer than they should, and my desk was never a model of order — but I got the important things done when they mattered. My temperament has always been on the calmer side
column2: crises rarely rattle me, and I tend to respond with measured, practical solutions rather than drama.

column1: Politically, I’ve been a Democrat for most of my adult life. My views are firmly liberal on the big issues: social safety nets, civil rights, the protection of liberties for marginalized people. I care deeply about access to quality education and sensible healthcare policies. Over the decades I followed every twist of policy and politics — committee hearings, local elections, Supreme Court decisions. I read history and policy journals, subscribed to newspapers, and listened to public radio. I like to think of myself as very knowledgeable about political issues and events
column2: knowing the facts and the history matters to me. I spend a significant portion of my information time in left-leaning sources, but I also make a point of reading opposing views, maybe twenty percent of my intake, so I understand the arguments against my own. That habit keeps me honest and helps me anticipate where compromises might come from.

column1: Yet I have never been a party acolyte. I vote Democrat because those policies align with my principles, but I do not blindly support every candidate or every strategy the party adopts. Over the years I became increasingly critical of party machinery when it seemed to trade principle for expediency. I prefer independent thinking
column2: when a candidate or platform looks like it’s straying from core values, I’ll say so. That independence has occasionally put me at odds with activists who expect unanimous support, but I value integrity over tribal loyalty.

column1: In personality, I am neither flashy nor avant-garde. I have traditional tastes and a preference for the familiar: a modest garden of roses and herbs rather than exotic plants, classical music and a few favorite novels over experimental art. I am warm in personal relationships but not uncritically so
column2: I’m the sort of person who listens and offers practical help rather than pouring out sentimental demonstrations. People tell me I can be blunt — true enough. I don’t always sugarcoat when something seems wrong, but I try to be fair.

column1: In retirement I’ve settled into a comfortable rhythm. Mornings begin with coffee and the paper
column2: I clip articles and write letters to my representatives when something matters deeply. I spend afternoons tending my garden, volunteering at the local library, and occasionally guest-lecturing at the community college. I have a small circle of friends and family I rely on, and a couple of grandchildren who bring a particular kind of joy. I keep up with new developments, but I don’t chase novelty for novelty’s sake
column3: if something is worth my attention, it earns it.

column1: Looking back, I’m proud of a life lived with curiosity, principle, and a certain quiet stubbornness. I haven’t been the loudest voice in the room, but I have kept my mind engaged and my values intact.
